q: What natural process do genetic algorithms imitate?
options: Biological evolution through natural selection
The way neurons in the brain pass signals to each other
The way an animal learns by being rewarded for its actions
The way metals cool slowly and settle into a stable structure
explain: Genetic algorithms are inspired by evolution. A population of solutions changes over generations, and the fitter ones are more likely to pass on their features.
source: Week 5 genetic algorithms lecture, slide 1 and 6

q:
Is the following statement about genetic algorithms correct?
"A genetic algorithm improves one single solution step by step until it is good enough."
options: Correct, because each generation contains only the single best solution
Incorrect, because it keeps a whole population and changes it each generation
Incorrect, because it never improves any solution and only picks at random
Correct, because crossover can be done using only one parent solution
explain: A genetic algorithm works on a population. It selects parents from the current population by fitness and uses them to produce children for the next generation.
source: Week 5 genetic algorithms lecture, slide 7

q: When a genetic algorithm represents a candidate solution as a bitstring, what does the whole bitstring correspond to?
options: A gene
A mutation
A chromosome
A fitness score
explain: A chromosome is the full string and each gene is one position in it, a 0 or a 1 in the bitstring example. Fitness is the score of the chromosome, not the string itself.
source: Week 5 genetic algorithms lecture, slide 2 and 14

q: When a candidate solution is stored as a bitstring, what is a single gene?
options: The whole string that represents the candidate
The number that the bitstring decodes to
The pair of parents chosen for crossover
One bit in the chromosome, with a value of 0 or 1
explain: Genes are the blocks that make up a chromosome. In the example each gene is a single bit.
source: Week 5 genetic algorithms lecture, slide 2 and 14

q: In a genetic algorithm, what does the fitness of a chromosome tell you?
options: How good that solution is at solving the problem
How many genes the chromosome contains
How different the chromosome is from its parents
How many generations the algorithm has run so far
explain: Fitness measures success. In biology it is how well an organism does, and here it is how good a solution is. It is used to decide which solutions are kept.
source: Week 5 genetic algorithms lecture, slide 2 and 15

q: Which operation in a genetic algorithm combines parts of two parent chromosomes to make a new one?
options: Mutation
Crossover
Fitness testing
Encoding
explain: Crossover is the recombination of genes from parents. Mutation instead changes bits at random in one chromosome.
source: Week 5 genetic algorithms lecture, slide 2, 4 and 16

q: What does mutation do to a chromosome in a genetic algorithm?
options: It joins it with a second parent to make a child
It deletes the weakest chromosomes from the population
It randomly changes part of it, such as flipping a bit
It scores it by how good a solution it is
explain: Mutation is a random change to the DNA or bitstring, like a copying error. It adds variety that crossover alone might not give.
source: Week 5 genetic algorithms lecture, slide 5 and 16
flag: The purpose of adding variety is standard knowledge, the slides define mutation as a random change.

q: How does a genetic algorithm start?
options: By differentiating an equation and finding where its gradient is zero
By choosing the single best solution from a stored list
By crossing over two parent solutions chosen by hand
By creating an initial population of random candidate solutions
explain: The first step generates a set of random solutions, encoded for example as bitstrings, and then tests how good each one is.
source: Week 5 genetic algorithms lecture, slide 13 and 14

q: Which actions are part of the repeating loop of a genetic algorithm?
options: Remove some of the bad solutions
Replace the whole population with new random solutions every time
Test and rank each solution by how good it is
Duplicate some of the good solutions
Make small changes to the good solutions
explain: The loop tests, removes weak solutions, duplicates strong ones and varies them until the best is good enough. Restarting at random each time would throw away what has been learned.
source: Week 5 genetic algorithms lecture, slide 13

q: When does the genetic algorithm loop stop?
options: When the best solution is good enough
After exactly one generation
When every chromosome has been mutated once
When the population has shrunk to a single chromosome
explain: The loop repeats until the best solution is good enough. It does not stop after a fixed single pass.
source: Week 5 genetic algorithms lecture, slide 13 and 15

q: Which are problems with solving an optimisation problem by differentiating an equation?
options: It is not suitable for complex real-world problems with many variables
Differentiation can only find maxima and never minima
It always needs a population of random solutions first
The relationship may have several minima
Not every relationship can be written as an equation
explain: The analytical method needs an equation, can be confused by several minima and does not scale to complex problems. It can find minima, and it does not need a population.
source: Week 5 genetic algorithms lecture, slide 11

topic: Limits of blind generate and test
q: What is the main weakness of blind generate and test as a numerical method?
options: It can only be used when the relationship is an exact equation
Its guesses ignore earlier results, so it may take too long to converge
It always finds a perfect solution but needs too much memory
It has no way to check how good each guess is, so it cannot compare them
explain: Blind guessing is basic trial and error, so it can be slow and can be misled by several minima. A genetic algorithm does better by building on good solutions.
source: Week 5 genetic algorithms lecture, slide 11 to 13

q: Why can a genetic algorithm do better than blind trial and error?
options: It tests only one solution at a time, so it needs less computation
It tests every possible solution, so it can never miss the best one
It keeps and varies good solutions, so it builds on earlier results
It ignores how good each solution is, so it avoids any bias
explain: Ranking, removing bad solutions, duplicating good ones and making small changes steers the search towards better answers instead of guessing blindly.
source: Week 5 genetic algorithms lecture, slide 13

q: How is a problem usually set up before a genetic algorithm is run on it?
options: As a search for the point where a gradient equals zero
As a search for one exact answer by checking every possible option in turn
As a search for the most diverse set of candidate solutions
As a search for the minimum of something, which marks an acceptable limit
explain: A genetic algorithm usually looks for the minimum of some quantity, which stands for an acceptable limit. Other kinds of problem are rewritten as minimisation problems to fit.
source: Week 5 genetic algorithms lecture, slide 8
flag: The slide gives minimisation as the usual set up and says other problems are reformulated to fit.

q: Which problems suit a genetic algorithm well?
options: Sorting a short list of numbers
Finding the best route between many places
Scheduling many tasks or people
Optimisation problems in finance
Reading an exact answer from a known formula
explain: Genetic algorithms are most successful on large search spaces such as scheduling, route optimisation and finance. A short list or a known formula needs no search.
source: Week 5 genetic algorithms lecture, slide 1

q: What is a main disadvantage of genetic algorithms?
options: It can be difficult to represent a problem as a genetic problem
They cannot find an approximate solution to any problem
They need the problem to be written as a differentiable equation
They can only work on problems with exactly one minimum
explain: Approximate solutions can usually be found, but the problem has to be encoded as chromosomes, which is not always easy. They do not need an equation and can cope with several minima.
source: Week 5 genetic algorithms lecture, slide 18

q: Which statements about genetic algorithm terms are correct?
options: Fitness is how successful or good an individual is
Mutation is a random change, like an error in copying a gene
A gene is the complete string that represents one candidate solution
Crossover recombines genes from parents
explain: Crossover mixes parent genes, mutation is a random change and fitness measures success. The complete string is the chromosome, and a gene is one block within it.
source: Week 5 genetic algorithms lecture, slide 2, 4 and 5

q: Explain what a genetic algorithm is and the main steps it follows.
model: A genetic algorithm solves optimisation problems by imitating biological evolution. It starts with a population of random candidate solutions, often encoded as bitstrings called chromosomes. Each solution is tested for fitness and ranked. The poor ones are removed and the good ones are duplicated and changed by crossover and mutation to form the next generation. This loop repeats over many generations until the best solution is good enough, so the population evolves towards an optimum.
points: Says it imitates biological evolution
Starts with a random population of encoded solutions
Describes testing for fitness and selecting the better solutions
Describes creating new solutions with crossover and mutation
Says the loop repeats until the best solution is good enough
source: Week 5 genetic algorithms lecture, slide 6, 7, 13 and 14

q: Describe the biological terms chromosome, gene and fitness and say what each means in a genetic algorithm.
model: In biology a chromosome is a string of DNA and a gene is a block of DNA that decides some feature of the organism. Fitness is how successful the organism is. In a genetic algorithm a chromosome is a candidate solution, often a bitstring. A gene is one position in it, such as a single bit with a value of 0 or 1. Fitness is how good the candidate solution is, and it decides which chromosomes are kept to produce the next generation.
points: Defines a chromosome as the string that represents a candidate solution
Defines a gene as a unit within the chromosome such as one bit
Defines fitness as how successful or good a solution is
Says what each term means in biology
source: Week 5 genetic algorithms lecture, slide 2 and 14

q: Compare crossover and mutation and explain why a genetic algorithm uses both.
model: Crossover combines genes from two parent chromosomes to make a child, in the same way that parents pass on a mixture of their DNA. Mutation makes a small random change, such as flipping one bit, like an error in copying a gene. Crossover mixes the good features that already exist in the population. Mutation introduces new variety that the existing solutions may not contain. Using both lets the algorithm keep what works while still exploring new possibilities.
points: Describes crossover as recombining genes from parents
Describes mutation as a random change to a gene or bit
Explains that crossover mixes existing features while mutation adds new variety
source: Week 5 genetic algorithms lecture, slide 4, 5 and 16
flag: The reason for using both is standard knowledge, the slides define each operator and use both in step 3.

topic: Limits of analytical and numerical methods
q: Explain why finding the minimum of a function by differentiation may not work for real problems, and how a genetic algorithm helps.
model: Differentiation needs the relationship to be written as an equation, and many real relationships cannot be. Some problems have several minima and many variables, which makes the analytical method unsuitable. Blind trial and error can work but may take too long and does not learn from earlier guesses. A genetic algorithm starts with random solutions, ranks them, drops poor ones, copies good ones and makes small changes. This guided search can find a good approximate answer without needing an equation.
points: Says not all relationships can be written as an equation
Mentions multiple minima or complex multivariable problems
Says blind generate and test can be too slow
Says a genetic algorithm gives a guided search and approximate answers
source: Week 5 genetic algorithms lecture, slide 9 to 13

q: Describe how a candidate solution can be represented in a genetic algorithm, using a bitstring as the example.
model: A candidate solution is encoded as a string of bits, which forms a chromosome. Each bit is a gene with a value of 0 or 1. For example, a six bit string can stand for a whole number x from 0 to 63, and the algorithm looks for the x that gives the lowest value of a chosen equation. The initial population is a set of random bitstrings. Each is decoded to a number and tested to measure its fitness.
points: Says the solution is encoded as a bitstring or chromosome
Says each bit is a gene with value 0 or 1
Says the string is decoded to a value that is tested for fitness
Mentions a random initial population
source: Week 5 genetic algorithms lecture, slide 14 and 15

q: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of genetic algorithms and say what kind of problem suits them.
model: An advantage is that approximate solutions can usually be found, even where no equation exists. A disadvantage is that it can be hard to represent a problem as a genetic problem, since it must first be encoded as chromosomes with a fitness measure. Genetic algorithms are most successful on large search spaces, such as scheduling, route optimisation and finance, where checking every option would be impractical.
points: States the advantage of finding approximate solutions
States the difficulty of encoding a problem
Names large search spaces and gives an example such as scheduling or routes
source: Week 5 genetic algorithms lecture, slide 1 and 18
